'''''Corylus americana''''', the '''American hazelnut'''<ref name="america">{{eFloras|1|233500448|Corylus americana |family=Betulaceae |first=John J. |last=Furlow}}</ref> or '''American hazel''',<ref name="GRIN">{{GRIN |access-date=2018-07-23}}</ref> is a species of [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] in the genus ''[[Corylus]]'', native to the [[eastern United States|eastern]] and [[central United States]] and extreme southern parts of eastern and central [[Canada]].<ref name="america" /><ref>{{BONAP |genus=Corylus |species=americana}}</ref>

==Description==
The American hazelnut grows to a height of roughly {{cvt|2.5|to|5|m|ft|0}},<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=c350 |title=Corylus americana |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |access-date=2016-07-05}}</ref>  with a crown spread of {{cvt|3|to|4.5|m|ft|0}}. It is a medium to large shrub, which under some conditions can take the likeness of a small tree. It is often multi-stemmed with long outward growing branches that form a dense spreading or spherical shape. It spreads by sending up [[sucker (botany)|suckers]] from underground [[rhizome]]s {{cvt|10|to|15|cm|0}} below the surface.<ref name="FEIS">{{FEIS |genus=Corylus |species=americana |type=shrub |last=Coladonato |first=Milo |date=1993}}</ref>

It blooms in very early<ref name="america" /> to mid spring,<ref name="Illinois">{{Illinois Wildflowers|trees/plants/am_hazelnut|American Hazelnut (Corylus americana)}}</ref> producing hanging male ([[staminate]]) [[catkin]]s {{cvt|4|to|8|cm|frac=4}} long, and clusters of 2–5<!-- the number of nuts per cluster -->  tiny female ([[pistillate]]) flowers enclosed in the protective [[bract]]s of a bud, with their red [[style (botany)|styles]] sticking out at the tip.<ref name="america" /><ref name="Minnesota">{{Minnesota Wildflowers|shrub/american-hazelnut|Corylus americana (American Hazelnut)}}</ref> The male catkins develop in the fall and remain over the winter. Each male flower on a catkin has a pair of bracts and four [[stamen]]s.<ref name="Illinois" /><ref name="FNA genus">{{eFloras|1|108088|Corylus |family=Betulaceae |first=John J. |last=Furlow}}</ref>

American hazelnut produces edible nuts that mature at a time between July and October. Each nut is enclosed in two leaf-like [[bract]]s<ref name="FNA genus" /> with irregularly [[laciniate]] [[leaf margin|margins]].<ref name="america" />

== Ecology ==
The nuts produced by American hazelnut are a [[Mast (botany)|mast]] of [[squirrel]]s, [[whitetail deer]], [[fox]]es, [[ruffed grouse]], [[northern bobwhite]]s, [[ring-necked pheasant|pheasant]]s, [[turkey (bird)|turkey]], [[woodpeckers]], and other animals. The leaves are browsed on by whitetail deer, [[moose]], and [[rabbit]]s. The male catkins are a food staple of ruffed grouse and turkey throughout the winter. The low-hanging shrubs form habitat for many animal species. {{Citation needed|date=June 2024}}

== Uses ==
The nuts are edible raw,<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|pages=173|oclc=244766414|orig-year=1982}}</ref> although smaller than the more commonly cultivated filberts (''[[Corylus maxima]]'',<ref name="america" /><ref name="hortus">{{Cite book|last1=Bailey|first1=Liberty Hyde|title=Hortus third : a concise dictionary of plants cultivated in the United States and Canada|last2=Bailey|first2=Ethel Zoe|publisher=Macmillan|year=1976|isbn=0-02-505470-8|location=New York|pages=479|oclc=2513407}}</ref> ''[[Corylus avellana]]'',<ref name="hortus"/> and hybrids thereof).<ref name="hortus"/> They also possess an oil content comparable to ''C. avellana'', making them well-suited to culinary oil production.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Xu |first1=Yixiang |last2=Hanna |first2=Milford A |date=2010-11-01 |title=Composition and oxidative stabilities of oils extracted from hybrid hazelnuts grown in Nebraska, USA |url=https://academic.oup.com/ijfst/article/45/11/2329/7865204 |journal=International Journal of Food Science and Technology |volume=45 |issue=11 |pages=2329–2336 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2621.2010.02404.x |issn=0950-5423|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

[[Indigenous people of the Americas|Native Americans]] used ''Corylus americana'' for medicinal purposes, such as hives, biliousness, diarrhea, cramps, hay fever, childbirth, hemorrhages, prenatal strength and teething, to induce vomiting and to heal cuts.<ref name="america" />

===Cultivation===
''Corylus americana'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] for [[native plant]] gardens, and in [[wildlife garden]]s to attract and keep fauna in an area. There are cultivated hybrids of ''Corylus americana'' with ''[[Corylus avellana]]'' which aim to combine the larger nuts of the latter with the former's resistance to a North American fungus ''[[Cryptosporella]] anomala''.<ref name="hortus"/>

It is a medium to fast-growing species, that suckers moderately, eventually producing a multi-stemmed, clump appearance.{{cn|date=October 2024}}

It adapts well to a range of soil pH and types, but does best on well-drained loams. American hazelnut prefers full sun for best growth and development. Though it can grow and persist in partial shade, plant density and fruit production are greatly reduced.{{cn|date=October 2024}}
